planting.note: Pot up nursery-grown offsets or seedlings in spring into very lean, gritty mineral mix; wear gloves, since any cut into the corky trunk releases a caustic latex that irritates skin and eyes.

directions: This slow-growing South African succulent forms a thick, corky, cone-shaped stem densely studded with spirally arranged rhomboid tubercles — the raised scars left by fallen leaves — giving mature specimens a texture reminiscent of a pinecone or pineapple. A loose rosette of narrow, spoon-shaped leaves crowns the growth point and is typically shed during hot dry spells or winter dormancy, leaving the sculptural bare trunk as the main ornamental feature for much of the year. Unlike the smooth-ribbed, melon-shaped stem of the related Euphorbia meloformis, bupleurifolia's surface is rough and knobby throughout, and older plants may branch low to form multiple heads. Grow in a shallow pot of very lean, gritty mineral mix with bright light and minimal water, and wear gloves when trimming or repotting since any cut releases a caustic milky latex that irritates skin and eyes.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America

San Marcos Growers

planting.note: Plant divisions of the tuberous rootstock in spring in extremely fast-draining grit; wear gloves, since the latex exuded from cut stems is a skin and eye irritant despite the species' historical use as a cooked food source.

directions: Known in its native Karoo region of South Africa as vingerpol, this clump-forming succulent produces a spreading mat of prostrate, finger-like, spineless stems that arise from a thickened underground tuberous rootstock rather than forming a single upright body. The Latin epithet esculenta ('edible') references a documented history of the tuber being roasted and eaten by indigenous peoples after careful processing to neutralize its otherwise toxic, skin-irritating latex — home gardeners should treat all parts as inedible and wear gloves when handling cut stems. Its low, spreading habit and gray-green, faintly mottled finger stems distinguish it from the upright columnar euphorbias more typically seen in cultivation. Site in full sun in extremely fast-draining, gritty soil and water only sparingly during the active growing season, allowing the tuber to stay nearly dry through winter dormancy.
sources: LLIFLE Encyclopedia of Succulents
Cactus and Succulent Society of America
Kew Plants of the World Online

planting.note: Divide offset clumps in spring and pot into very well-drained gritty mix; wear gloves, since broken stems ooze a caustic latex that irritates skin and eyes.

directions: One of the smallest euphorbias grown in cultivation, Superstition Plant forms dense, slow-spreading mounds of miniature, spirally tuberculate stem segments rarely more than an inch or two tall, each individual head resembling a tiny pinecone or clustered popcorn kernel. Completely spineless, it relies on offsetting rather than height to spread, eventually filling a shallow pot with hundreds of tightly packed heads over many years. Small pale flowers appear at the tips of the outermost segments in the growing season, and the plant is native to the semi-arid Eastern Cape of South Africa. Provide bright light, extremely well-drained gritty mix, and sparing water, and handle broken stems with gloves, since the exposed latex is an eye and skin irritant like other Euphorbia species.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America
LLIFLE Encyclopedia of Succulents
Huntington Botanical Gardens Desert Collection

planting.note: Take offset cuttings in spring, let the cut end callus for several days, then pot in fast-draining mix; wear gloves, since the sap released when dividing offsets is a skin and eye irritant.

directions: Corncob Euphorbia forms clustering columns of gray-green stems covered in tight spiraling rows of small nipple-like tubercles, each tipped with a slender dried flower stalk that persists as a short soft spine, together producing the ridged, corn-on-the-cob texture that gives the plant its common name. Offsets form readily at the base, and over time a single plant develops into a broad clump of upright fingers rather than a solitary trunk, distinguishing it from the smoother, unribbed stems of Euphorbia trigona. It tolerates light frost better than many succulent euphorbias but still needs protection below freezing, and thrives with bright light and minimal water in fast-draining mineral soil. As with the rest of the genus, any broken stem exudes a caustic milky sap, so wear gloves when dividing offsets or taking cuttings.
sources: San Marcos Growers
LLIFLE Encyclopedia of Succulents
Cactus and Succulent Society of America

planting.note: Root short stem-segment cuttings in spring after callusing in dry gritty mix; wear gloves, since the milky sap from cut stems is a skin and eye irritant.

directions: Often confused with the closely related Euphorbia globosa, this South African species forms sprawling, low clusters of cylindrical, blue-green stems marked with spiraling rows of small tubercles, branching and creeping along the soil surface before individual segments curve upward. It lacks spines entirely, and small yellow-green cyathia appear near the growing tips during the warmer months, adding subtle seasonal interest to what is primarily a foliage and form succulent. The loosely sprawling, mat-forming habit distinguishes it from the more tightly rounded, ball-like segments typical of true globosa, making it useful trailing over the edge of a container. Grow in bright light with excellent drainage and minimal water, and wear gloves when handling since the sap is a skin and eye irritant typical of the genus.

planting.note: Handle only nursery-propagated offsets in spring, potting into scrupulously well-drained grit; wear gloves near the spine clusters and because the latex sap is a caustic skin and eye irritant.

directions: Star Spine Euphorbia forms a solitary or slowly clustering, ribbed, globose-to-cylindrical stem armed along each rib with evenly spaced clusters of spines that radiate outward in a distinct star pattern, a feature that separates it at a glance from the straighter, paired spines of the similar-looking African Milk Barrel, Euphorbia horrida. Extremely slow growing even by succulent-euphorbia standards, it can take many years to reach a modest clumping specimen and is prized by specialist collectors for that architectural spine pattern as much as for the plant's overall form. Native to the semi-arid Cape regions of South Africa, it demands scrupulous drainage and minimal water to avoid rot, particularly during cool winter months. Handle with gloves when repotting or propagating, since the milky latex sap released from any wound is a caustic irritant to skin and eyes.
sources: LLIFLE Encyclopedia of Succulents

IUCN Red List of Threatened Species

planting.note: Only pot nursery-propagated plants in spring into a shallow pan of almost pure mineral grit; wear gloves, since the sap is a skin and eye irritant, and keep this rot-prone species nearly dry through cool weather.

directions: Named for its uncanny resemblance to a small globular Gymnocalycium cactus, this rare dwarf species from the highlands of Ethiopia forms a flattened, gray-green globose body marked with faint mottling and broad, low ribs, usually growing solitary or offsetting only sparingly with age. It stays only a few inches across even in old specimens, making it one of the most compact euphorbias grown by specialist collectors, who prize it for its cactus-like silhouette combined with typical Euphorbia flower and sap traits. Because it is exceptionally prone to rot, it should be grown in a shallow pot of almost pure mineral grit with minimal organic matter and watered only when fully dry, ideally with extra winter protection from cold, damp conditions. As with all euphorbias, any cut or scrape releases a milky latex that is a significant skin and eye irritant, so gloves are essential when handling or repotting.
sources: IUCN Red List of Threatened Species

planting.note: Root stem cuttings in spring after the cut end has callused in dry, gritty mix; wear gloves when pruning the spiny stems, since the sap is a caustic skin and eye irritant.

directions: Unlike the leafless globular euphorbias more commonly grown as succulents, this shrubby Madagascar species retains persistent, leathery, elongated leaves along thick, spine-studded stems, giving it a coarser, more traditionally shrub-like appearance year-round. Dense clusters of small but vividly red-to-orange cyathia are produced at the stem tips for much of the growing season, providing color reminiscent of the related crown-of-thorns, Euphorbia milii, but on a heavier-textured, more robustly spined plant. It is part of a distinct group of Madagascar spiny shrub euphorbias valued in succulent collections for combining true foliage with long-blooming color. Grow in full sun with excellent drainage and moderate water during active growth, and handle pruning cuts with gloves, since the sap is a caustic skin and eye irritant characteristic of the genus.
sources: Missouri Botanical Garden Plant Finder
